tagline: Mainland roads and island causeways link lagoon towns with protected shores.
intro: The Indian River Lagoon National Scenic Byway runs along both sides of the lagoon, joining US 1 and coastal A1A with causeways. Florida’s scenic-highways program lists 233 miles, with state designation in 2000 and national designation in 2002. The program highlights protected barrier-island habitats at Merritt Island, Canaveral National Seashore and Archie Carr, beside the Kennedy Space Center. At Cocoa, the network includes CR 515, a slower two-lane residential road directly beside the Indian River.

Before railroads arrived, the lagoon was an essential transportation link. Road bridges changed the connections between its shores: the Melbourne Causeway joined Melbourne Beach to the mainland through Indialantic in 1921. At Titusville, a swing bridge built in 1949 was replaced in 2011 by the fixed, high-level A. Max Brewer Bridge. That crossing connects the city to Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge and Canaveral National Seashore.

Begin north of Titusville and follow the mainland strand through Cocoa toward Melbourne and Sebastian. To connect the stops below, cross at the Melbourne Causeway, then turn south on A1A past Melbourne Beach toward Sebastian Inlet. McLarty Treasure Museum occupies part of the fleet survivors’ camp site south of the inlet; beyond it, Pelican Island’s visitor facilities lie west of A1A on Historic Jungle Trail. The coastal strand continues to Wabasso Beach.

moments.title: Cocoa
moments.text: One of Cocoa’s naming stories begins with mail delivered by riverboat. One account says letters were left in a Baker’s Cocoa tin nailed to a river piling beside downtown. A fire destroyed most of the business district in 1890; the extension of the Jacksonville, St. Augustine, and Indian River Railway subsequently stimulated development. The historic downtown, Cocoa Village, reaches Riverfront Park along the Indian River. Its former post office, built by the Works Progress Administration in 1939, now houses the Florida Historical Society. Cocoa Village’s historic playhouse began as the Aladdin Theatre.

moments.title: McLarty Treasure Museum
moments.text: The McLarty Treasure Museum occupies part of a camp used by survivors and salvagers of the 1715 Spanish treasure fleet. The fleet was trying to return to Spain when a hurricane struck off Florida’s coast. The survivors’ camp site entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1970. Robert McLarty, a retired Atlanta attorney living in Vero Beach, donated the museum property to the state. The museum exhibits wreck-related artifacts and has an observation deck overlooking the Atlantic. The museum is part of Sebastian Inlet State Park, on the barrier island at the north end of Indian River County.
moments.notice: The museum’s observation deck looks over the Atlantic Ocean.

moments.title: Pelican Island
moments.text: Pelican Island became the nation’s first national wildlife refuge by Theodore Roosevelt’s executive order on March 14, 1903. Plume hunters killed birds for feathers used in women’s hats. Paul Kroegel sailed out to guard the birds, and Frank Chapman and William Dutcher appealed to Roosevelt for protection. Centennial visitor facilities added in 2003 included a boardwalk and observation tower for viewing the island. The nesting island itself does not allow visitors to disembark. The refuge also includes a section of Historic Jungle Trail, a sandy road built by citrus growers in the 1920s.
